extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office personnel (patent examiners) and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness of claimed chemical compounds and related obviousness rationales (lead compound, known technique, obvious-to-try) under Graham/KSR principles. Focuses on the factual findings required and how to treat secondary considerations and predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead compound obviousness (structural similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness based on structural similarity can be proved by identification of some motivation that would have led one of ordinary skill in the art to select and then modify a known compound (i.e. a lead compound) in a particular way to achieve the claimed compound. ... it is sufficient to show that the claimed and prior art compounds possess a ‘sufficiently close relationship ... to create an expectation,' in light of the totality of the prior art, that the new compound will have ‘similar properties’ to the old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requisite motivation may come from any number of sources and need not necessarily be explicit in the art. Office personnel should consider whether the prior art taught modifying the lead compound in the claimed way and whether that modification would have been expected to yield similar properties. Structural similarity alone is insufficient without a reason to select and modify the prior art compound and a reasonable expectation of success. Example: Eisai (lead compound characterized) and Altana/Procter & Gamble discussions illustrate need for both a reason to modify and reasonable expectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual meaning and selection of 'lead compound'
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'lead compound' in judicial opinions can have a contextual meaning that may vary from the way a pharmaceutical chemist might use the term. Any known compound might possibly serve as a lead compound for obviousness, including inactive compounds, if there is a reason for starting with that compound other than mere existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel are cautioned that a compound not considered a 'lead' by chemists (for being inactive, expensive, difficult to handle, or for business reasons) might nonetheless be used as a lead compound in an obviousness analysis. However, there must be some reason to select and modify that particular compound beyond the mere fact that it exists. Case citations: Eisai; Altana Pharma AG v. Teva; Ortho-McNeil Pharm. v. Mylan Labs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to articulate reason to select and modify a lead compound
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be some reason 'to select and modify a known compound' to support an obviousness rejection based on a lead compound rationale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting obviousness from a lead compound, examiners must identify the motivating factors (explicit or implicit in the prior art) that would have led one of ordinary skill to choose that starting compound and to make the claimed modification. Reasons may derive from the totality of the prior art, expert opinion, or other sources; mere existence of the prior compound is insufficient. See Altana Pharma AG v. Teva, and related Federal Circuit precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of unexpected results and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Unexpected results (e.g., unexpectedly superior potency or lower toxicity) can rebut a prima facie case of obviousness. Commercial success and meeting a long-felt but unsatisfied need are relevant secondary considerations, but their weight depends on circumstances (e.g., commercial success given little weight if competing product was assigned to same assignee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should consider evidence of unexpected results demonstrated by comparative tests, witness credibility, and magnitude of improvement. Evaluate commercial success and long-felt need as of the filing date of the challenged invention. Example: Procter & Gamble v. Teva—unexpected potency/toxicity results rebutted obviousness; commercial success given limited weight because competing product was also assigned to petitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of a single lead compound not always required
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead compound cases do not stand for the proposition that identification of a single lead compound is necessary in every obviousness rejection of a chemical compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate bases for obviousness may include prior art suggestions to formulate compounds having certain structurally defined moieties or viewing a claimed compound as two known compounds linked by a chemical linker. If one of ordinary skill would have known how to synthesize such a compound and the structural/functional result would have been reasonably predictable, a prima facie case of obviousness might exist without a single identified lead compound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Known Technique To Improve Similar Devices (methods or products)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on applying a known technique to improve similar devices, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) a finding that the prior art contained a 'base' device; (2) a finding that the prior art contained a 'comparable' device that has been improved in the same way as the claimed invention; (3) a finding that one of ordinary skill could have applied the known 'improvement' technique in the same way to the 'base' device and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a method of enhancing a class of devices has become part of ordinary capabilities, so applying it to a base device would have been predictable. Cite KSR: if actual application would have been beyond skill, then not obvious. Example support: Intel Corp. v. PACT XPP Schweiz AG (both references address same problem; motivation to combine under KSR). If any of the four findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying a Known Technique to a Known Device Ready for Improvement (predictable results)
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim under this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) that the prior art contained a 'base' device; (2) that the prior art contained a known technique applicable to the base device; (3) that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that applying the known technique would have yielded predictable results and an improved system; and (4) any additional Graham findings necessary to explain obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: the known technique is part of ordinary skill, and applying it to a device ready for improvement would yield predictable outcomes. If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot be used. Examples: Dann v. Johnston (application of indicia on data to allow predictable sorting/reporting); In re Nilssen (use of threshold signal to actuate cutoff switch); In re Urbanski (combination of reaction times where result-effective variables were recognized).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Obvious to Try"—finite identified predictable solutions with reasonable expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: To reject a claim based on an 'obvious to try' rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate: (1) that a recognized problem or need existed at the relevant time; (2) that a finite number of identified, predictable potential solutions to the problem existed; (3) that one of ordinary skill could have pursued the known potential solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; and (4) any additional Graham findings necessary to explain obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: a skilled person has reason to pursue known options and, if success was expected, the result may reflect ordinary skill. Courts emphasize predictability and reasonable expectation of success; mere 'obvious to try' without predictability is insufficient. Consider characteristics of the science/technology, state of advance, specificity of prior art, and predictability of results (Abbott Labs. v. Sandoz caution). Examples: Pfizer v. Apotex (finite set of pharmaceutically acceptable salts gave reasonable expectation); courts have applied this especially in chemical arts but require careful, context-specific analysis. If any required finding cannot be made, do not use this rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve Graham factual inquiries before applying any rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries (scope and content of prior art; differences between prior art and claims; level of ordinary skill; and objective evidence) before applying lead compound, known technique, or obvious-to-try rationales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All of the specific rationales (lead compound, known technique, obvious to try) are contingent upon first addressing the Graham factors. Additional findings based on those inquiries may be necessary for a proper explanation of obviousness in view of the facts of the case.
